rv.q: English, Sanaz Toossi's stunning Broadway debut, is a precise study of language's significance.
The performances still have the bloom of freshness and discovery, in exploring both the characters' sympathies and antipathies.

How our mother tongue gives us voice yet limits our world — and how a new tongue expands that world yet may strangle our voice — is the subject of “English,” a rich new play by Sanaz Toossi that opened on Tuesday at the Linda Gross Theater.

Now they return to The Daughter-in-Law, a strange and compelling portrait of a misalliance. The marriage between Minnie (Amy Blackman) and miner Luther Gascoyne (Tom Coiner) is only seven weeks old, but it’s already bubbling with betrayal and class-confusion.
That one play can accomplish as much with wit, ease, precision, and heart, as English does in a swift 115 minutes, makes it among the best new plays of the season.
English is an outstanding play that compellingly examines the weight of language on those burdened with carrying more than one, and the difficulty of communicating yourself to a changing world.
Between this intensely focused and sensitive staging and his no-less powerful handling of Primary Trust, Adams must be on top of every young playwright's vision board.
Through these five differing lenses, Toossi makes sharp and penetrating observations on how language shapes one's attitude to self-worth, environment and society.
As in life, there are no clear-cut lessons in English — and that makes it well worth your time.
Sanaz Toossi's English is a fascinating little play.
But their efforts are not enough to prevent you from desperately wanting to cut this class.
Over the course of the play, under Knud Adams' careful direction, English reveals itself to be an exquisitely crafted production.
English is one of those 'must-see' plays that makes you think about the space you occupy in the world.

cn.t: Toossi's Pulitzer-winning play earns strong praise as a deceptively simple comedy about learning English that deepens into a moving exploration of identity, assimilation, and loss. Critics laud the sharp direction and performances, though some find the pacing tedious.
